speaker: Petter Hörnfeldt
title: Ep16 - Interview with Petter Hoernfeldt - Mentour Pilot
question: In commercial aviation, why do many pilots end up regretting the move from short-haul to long-haul flying once they finally qualify for it?
guest: When you start your training, you try to get your first job, and that's always the hardest because of a catch-22 where employers want experience, but to get experience you need a job. So your first job tends to be short to medium haul, flying mail at night, or cargo—whatever you can get—while everyone still thinks, 'I want to fly long haul.' Actually, the best time to do that is in your early twenties, but no one gets the chance because you need more experience for long-haul jobs. So people treat short-haul jobs as stepping stones. By the time they gather enough experience, they can apply for long haul, but this is also when you tend to meet your spouse and start thinking about a family. Suddenly long-haul jobs become a problem because you're away from your family, away on weekends, and away for long periods. Instead of that glimmering goal from age 18, you wish you were back in short-to-medium haul with a set roster, no overnights, and coming home every night. Many people chase the slightly higher long-haul salary without realizing it's really about life quality—sometimes it's better to stay short haul and aim for long haul later once children have grown up.

points.core: Long-haul roles require flight experience that early-career pilots typically lack.
points.note: Accept: seniority or flight-hour barriers prevent young pilots in their early twenties from accessing widebody/long-haul seats when they have the fewest personal ties. Do not credit: generic remarks that long-haul jobs are competitive or prestigious.

points.core: Qualifying for long-haul usually coincides with starting a family.
points.note: Accept: pilots typically become eligible for long-haul in their late twenties or thirties right when they marry, have children, or take on major home responsibilities, making multi-day trips and weekend absences painful. Do not credit: vague statements that priorities change with age without linking to family/home life.

points.core: Short-haul flying offers more predictable rosters with nights spent at home.
points.note: Accept: short-to-medium haul provides steadier schedules, fewer or no overnight layovers, and returning home every night. Do not credit: generic claims that short-haul is easier or less tiring without mentioning schedule/home-at-night structure.

points.core: Deferring long-haul until children grow up better preserves pilot quality of life.
points.note: Accept: staying short-haul during child-rearing years and transitioning to long-haul later in one's career instead of chasing slightly higher pay early; prioritizing lifestyle over prestige/salary. Do not credit: both-sides hedging that either choice is fine depending on the person.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
It's not well established that "many" pilots regret the move: preferences split, and plenty of pilots prefer long-haul for its better pay, more days off in a block and fewer early starts. Those who do regret it tend to cite the same few reasons.

The biggest is fatigue. Constant time-zone changes, overnight flights and disrupted circadian rhythms leave some pilots feeling permanently jet-lagged, with days off spent recovering rather than living. There are also long-term health concerns around sleep disruption and cosmic radiation exposure.

The second is the flying itself. A long-haul pilot might make only a few takeoffs and landings a month, shared among an augmented crew, with hours of cruise monitoring in between. Pilots who enjoyed four hands-on sectors a day can find it dull and worry about their manual flying skills fading.

The third is lifestyle. Short-haul often means being home most nights, while long-haul means multi-day trips, missed family events and lonely hotel layovers.

Finally, moving fleets can reset seniority, which may mean worse rosters, reserve duty and a long wait as a first officer or relief pilot before regaining command.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: While long-haul flying carries prestige, larger aircraft, and higher pay, many pilots find the reality far more punishing than expected. The biggest shock is chronic circadian disruption: crossing multiple time zones back-to-back and trying to sleep in onboard crew bunks leaves pilots perpetually fatigued, often spending much of their time off at home simply recovering from jet lag rather than enjoying family life. Switching to widebodies also erodes relative bidding power, dropping a senior short-haul pilot—who previously enjoyed preferred schedules, frequent nights in their own bed, or even a captain’s seat—to the bottom of the long-haul seniority list, which brings reserve duty, missed holidays, and multi-day absences. Meanwhile, the romanticized international layovers of decades past have largely shrunk to brief, isolating rests in hotels. Finally, many miss hands-on flying: because augmented three- or four-pilot crews divide duties across marathon cruises, pilots endure long stretches of monotonous autopilot monitoring while logging only one or two landings a month, sometimes needing simulator sessions just to maintain basic landing currency.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A lot of pilots find that long-haul is more glamorous in theory than in practice. The biggest complaint is how little actual flying they get to do. A short-haul pilot might make four takeoffs and landings a day, but a long-haul pilot might manage only a few a month. Long flights carry augmented crews who share the sectors, and a junior first officer or cruise relief pilot may hardly ever land the aircraft. Hands-on skills can fade, and some airlines send pilots back to the simulator just to keep them current. Most of the job becomes monitoring systems through long, dull hours in cruise.

The lifestyle also costs more than expected. Overnight flights, crossing many time zones and irregular rest disrupt pilots' body clocks, causing chronic fatigue, poor sleep and possible long-term health effects. Trips last several days, so they miss more family events, and the novelty of layovers in exotic cities wears off when they're spent sleeping off jet lag in a hotel. Finally, a pilot who moves to a widebody fleet usually starts near the bottom of its seniority list, so they get the worst rosters. Training bonds and slower promotion to captain can also make it hard to switch back.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Many pilots who chase the prestige, higher pay, and exotic layovers of long-haul widebody flying quickly discover that the lifestyle comes with steep hidden costs. The biggest shock is chronic circadian disruption: constantly crossing time zones and flying through the body’s biological night creates persistent fatigue that short-haul rosters rarely match, taking a measurable toll on sleep and long-term health. Being away from home for days at a time also strains family and social life, turning glamorous destinations into lonely hotel stays while short-haul peers sleep in their own beds most nights. Inside the cockpit, the flying itself can feel surprisingly unfulfilling. Because long-haul pilots spend hours monitoring automated systems at cruise and perform only a handful of takeoffs and landings each month, many miss the hands-on flying and variety of busy multi-sector days. Finally, transitioning to a widebody fleet often drops a pilot to the bottom of that fleet’s bidding seniority, leaving them with worse schedules, fewer holidays off, and a slower upgrade to captain.

Pilots who regret the move often find that long-haul flying costs them more usable time at home than they expected. Overnight flights and repeated time-zone changes disrupt sleep, and part of a stretch of days off can go to recovering from jet lag. Multi-day trips can also mean missing more family routines, even when the roster gives them more days off on paper.

The flying itself changes, too. Short-haul crews may fly several legs in a day, with frequent departures, approaches and landings. On long-haul routes, much of the flight is spent monitoring systems in cruise, and on flights with relief crews, pilots may go several trips between landings they fly themselves. For pilots who enjoyed the pace and hands-on flying of short-haul work, the appeal of bigger aircraft and overseas layovers can wear off quickly.

Long-haul flying can mean fewer takeoffs and landings but more nights away from home. Pilots who enjoy the pace of short-haul work may find that one departure, hours of monitoring the cruise, and one arrival give them less of the hands-on flying they enjoy. Overnight flights and time-zone changes can also make it hard to sleep, and part of a stretch of days off may go toward recovering from jet lag.

Seniority can compound the trade-off. At some airlines, a pilot who had enough seniority to choose preferred short-haul trips may initially have little choice of routes or days off on the long-haul fleet. For pilots who valued getting home most nights and having a say in their schedule, those everyday benefits can turn out to matter more than the bigger aircraft or distant destinations.
